title: ASP.NET Core perf effort: summary of open performance PRs
body:
# ASP.NET Core perf effort: summary of open performance PRs

> **Status: nothing is merged yet.** Everything below is an open PR awaiting maintainer review. The numbers are expected improvements from those PRs, not shipped gains.

## Approach
- AI agent sessions ("workers") are each assigned one area of ASP.NET Core. They check existing PRs first to avoid duplicating work.
- Workers read the hot paths to find avoidable allocation and CPU work. They measure each candidate with BenchmarkDotNet A/B runs (main vs. PR, 3 interleaved rounds with MemoryDiagnoser).
- A candidate becomes a PR only if its benchmark shows a measurable win. Candidates whose gains are too small to matter are dropped.
- Each win gets one focused PR, with no public API or behavior changes and no unsafe code (see Rules below).
- A periodic automated, read-only check ("triage") runs about every 20 minutes and covers CI, review threads and conflicts for every open perf PR. A worker is started to fix or answer each PR it flags. Real CI failures are fixed. Flaky failures are retriggered with an empty commit plus a comment explaining the evidence.
- Nothing is merged without maintainer review and approval.
- All agents (coordinator and workers) ran on Claude Opus 5.5 (claude-opus-5.5) via GitHub Copilot.

## Human involvement: it wasn't magic or hands-off

My involvement wasn't just supplying a prompt. I was setting constraints, asking for measurements, and providing engineering judgment throughout the run. Here are some actual messages, with spelling preserved.

**Defining the work and requiring evidence**
> Look for more opportunities to improve the performance of the whole stack. Go component by component and do it, measure, test, experiment and then make a PR if it's good. Use minimum of 5 concurrent sessions to do this work

**Keeping compatibility in scope**
> Consider breaking changes. We don’t want to change public APIs to breaking changes. We can consider new APIs but that’s a hassle as well. Stick to internal implementation that we can optimize.

**Flagging the risks behind an optimization**
> Changing object lifetimes, pooling are possible but consider data exposed to callers or customers

**Reinforcing correctness**
> Consider also that we need to make sure PRs are green, it has to work not just be fast

**Applying engineering judgment**
> We're trying to avoid as much unsafe code as possible. Better to build on really efficient BCL primitives instead of custom vectorization in most cases. Only extremely isoalted casses warrant it

## Rules
Every change and every worker follows these rules:
- No public API, breaking or behavior changes.
- Pool or cache only when nothing pooled or cached is reachable by callers or leaks between requests.
- No unsafe code. Prefer BCL primitives such as `SearchValues`, `IndexOfAny` and `Ascii`.
- Each change ships with A/B benchmarks (3 interleaved rounds with MemoryDiagnoser) and passing tests.
- Comments and PR descriptions posted by workers end with an AI-agent signature.

## Executive summary
An AI-agent-driven effort to cut allocation and CPU overhead on ASP.NET Core hot paths, one component at a time.
- **93 open PRs** across 10 areas. Each is small and focused, comes with its own BenchmarkDotNet A/B results, and is designed to make no public API, breaking or behavior changes.
- **About the numbers:** headline figures are BenchmarkDotNet microbenchmarks of the specific code path changed (main vs. PR, interleaved A/B runs with MemoryDiagnoser). They are not end-to-end application throughput.
- **CI:** green on all open PRs except:
  - 5 PRs whose only failing leg is `aspnetcore-components-e2e`, which also fails on main. `Build Analysis` and `Build Insights` are red on those PRs only because of that leg.
  - #70209, whose CI is still running.
- **Reviews:** all review threads have been answered, either with a fix and a commit link or with evidence. Some are left open for a maintainer to decide.
- **Merging:** a PR is merged only after a maintainer approves it and CI is green. None are approved yet.
- **Next:** 4 parallel workers are looking for wins in the Identity stack. They have opened 10 Identity and auth PRs so far (#70218 and #70220–#70228), listed under Identity and Security / auth in the full PR list.

## Areas and changes
| Area | PRs | What changed |
|---|---|---|
| Kestrel / HTTP/2 / HTTP/3 | 8 | No string allocation for Content-Length, HPACK hashing, header append and validation fast paths, lazy HTTP/3 buffers |
| HTTP abstractions / headers / forms | 14 | Content-type fast paths, single-pass query and cookie decoding, multipart reads without MemoryStream, header formatting |
| Routing | 6 | DFA (deterministic finite automaton) matcher candidate sharing and pruning, policy edge building, link generation |
| Middleware | 16 | Response compression, output and response caching, CORS, static files and assets, logging, forwarded headers, rate limiting |
| Security / DataProtection / auth | 14 | Managed encryptor and AES-GCM in-place writes, TicketSerializer, authorization handler enumeration, bearer token authentication, ticket protection |
| MVC / Razor Pages | 11 | Model binding and validation, view rendering and lookup, content negotiation, tag helpers |
| Identity | 7 | PasswordValidator, UserValidator, UserManager construction, TOTP (time-based one-time password) and Base32, metrics and logger caching |
| Blazor / Components | 7 | RenderBatchWriter, keyed diff, SSR (server-side rendering) text writer, JS interop buffers |
| SignalR | 8 | Protocol parsing, hub activation, client target lookup, groups, streaming |
| OpenAPI | 2 | Resolving references, caching attribute lookups |

**Identity**
- #70174: Identity metrics cache
- #70175: SecurityStampValidator logger cache
- #70222: UserManager construction (about 104 B less per construction, 4.23 KB → 4.13 KB per resolve)
- #70223: PasswordValidator without LINQ (~240 ns/832 B → ~17 ns/72 B per valid password)
- #70224: UserValidator with cached SearchValues and a shared EmailAddressAttribute (~143 ns/320 B → ~84 ns/296 B, about −42%)
- #70226: TOTP validation reuses one HMAC and input buffer across timesteps. About 21% faster on a match and 35% faster on a miss; 520 B → 352 B per failed validation for modifier-based providers. **Trade-off:** the authenticator-app path (no modifier) goes from 0 B to about 296 B per validation, in exchange for about 2 µs less CPU.
- #70227: Base32.FromBase32 with range checks and a 5-bit accumulator (~230 ns → ~49 ns per authenticator key, about 4.6× faster)

### Status
- #70152, #70156, #70163, #70182 and #70203 fail only `aspnetcore-components-e2e`, which also fails on main. `Build Analysis` and `Build Insights` are red on these PRs only because of that leg. Each PR has an evidence comment.
- #70146 and #70218 are green.
- #70209 has CI running.
- #70160 is a draft. #70179 is on hold pending a design decision.

### Incidents and lessons
- A CI retrigger once pushed a commit with an empty tree. It was rolled back, and retriggers now verify the diff before and after pushing.
- A full-repo restore filled the disk. Workers now build only the projects they need.
- Long blocking waits stalled workers. Builds and benchmarks now run in the background with capped retries.
- Recurring flaky tests: `CanResolveServices`, Blazor Virtualization, `NavigationLock` and `VariableHeight_HtmlTable` E2E, and Kestrel `Http2 StreamPool`.
- The first #70146 benchmark measured CNG instead of the managed path on Windows. It now pins the managed encryptor configuration.

### In progress: Identity stack
Four parallel workers are covering the areas below. The 10 Identity and auth PRs (#70218 and #70220–#70228) came from this work.
1. SignInManager, UserManager, the claims principal factory and SecurityStampValidator.
2. Extensions.Core: password hasher, TOTP, token providers and passkeys.
3. Cookie auth, ticket serialization, authorization and the EF Core stores.
4. MapIdentityApi, bearer tokens and Identity UI.

</details>

**🤖 Posted by ASP.NET Core Perf 2 (AI Agent)**
